title: 🪑 The Office Desk Is Quietly Coming Back
part1:
The office is making room for an old idea: a desk that belongs to you.

In some workplaces, assigned desks are returning. Companies are reducing their reliance on hot-desking, a system in which workers are not given a personal desk and use whichever desk is free.

Some companies are connected to this quiet shift, according to one report.

The change comes as employees express dissatisfaction with hot-desking. One report points to several concerns. The office may compare poorly with a home workspace. Workers may sit close to unfamiliar colleagues. The daily work setting may also feel less predictable and consistent.
part2:
Hot-desking has still grown since before the pandemic. One discussion, citing survey data, put the share of employees using hot-desking at 20%—twice the pre-pandemic level.

Now, some employers are asking a different question: should every desk be shared?

For some offices, the answer is no. They are bringing back assigned seating, at least in selected workplaces. But this is not a full return to the old office. The wider market is still moving toward shared desks.
point_one_heading: A desk can shape the workday
point_one_body: One reason the desk matters may be psychological, not practical. In one survey, 87% of workers with assigned desks reported a sense of belonging at work, compared with 74% of workers without assigned desks. The gap in reported ability to concentrate was also clear: 80% versus 67%. These figures show an association, not proof that assigned desks caused the difference.
point_two_heading: A quiet return inside a bigger shift
point_two_body: The broader office market is still built around sharing. One report found that the share of companies with one desk per employee, or more, fell from 56% in 2023 to 40% in 2024. Respondents expected the figure to reach about one-third by 2026. So the return of assigned desks is a selective adjustment, not a market-wide reversal.
in_one_line: The assigned desk is not taking over the office again. It is reappearing as a quiet counter-move to hot-desking, while the wider workplace continues to share more desks.
